# Releases · honojs/hono

Hono v4.13.0 is now available!

The highlight of this release is performance: a batch of low-level optimizations makes the core request/response path significantly faster — up to 1.25x on common routes in our benchmark. This release also adds first-class support for the HTTP QUERY method, defined in [RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10008.html), a new Method Not Allowed middleware, and more.

## Performance improvements

This release includes a series of small optimizations: skipping unnecessary `Headers` allocations, replacing regex tests with `indexOf`, allocating internal state lazily, and more.

Here is [`benchmarks/fetch`](https://github.com/honojs/hono/tree/main/benchmarks/fetch) comparing v4.12 and v4.13 (`ROUNDS=5 ./compare.sh`, Bun 1.4.0, Apple Silicon — each measurement runs in a fresh process, and the variant order is reversed every round to avoid warm-up bias):

Benchmark

v4.12

v4.13

Speedup

`ping` — `GET /`

165.83 ns

163.99 ns

1.01x

`query` — `GET /id/1?name=bun`

674.40 ns

616.99 ns

**1.09x**

`json` — `GET /user`

528.99 ns

422.44 ns

**1.25x**

`body` — `POST /json`

1.16 µs

1.00 µs

**1.15x**

The individual changes:

*   perf(context): iterate the header record with `for..in` [#5118](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5118)
*   perf(url): replace regex tests with `indexOf` [#5121](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5121)
*   perf(context): skip `Headers` creation when there are no headers to merge [#5122](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5122)
*   perf(urls): refactor `tryDecodeURIComponent` [#5158](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5158)
*   perf(request): allocate `#validatedData` lazily [#5175](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5175)
*   perf(request): probe the body cache without allocating [#5176](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5176)

In addition, the RegExpRouter rewrite described below makes route registration plus the first match roughly 20% faster.

Thanks [@kibertoad](https://github.com/kibertoad) for the contributions!

## First-class QUERY method support

The QUERY method — a safe, idempotent method that carries a request body — is now a first-class citizen in Hono. You can define QUERY handlers with `app.query()`:

const app \= new Hono()

app.query('/search', async (c) \=> {
  const conditions \= await c.req.json()
  return c.json(await search(conditions))
})

Thanks [@shellhaki](https://github.com/shellhaki)!

## QUERY support across built-in middleware

The built-in middleware has been updated to handle QUERY requests properly:

### Cache Middleware

The Cache Middleware now caches QUERY responses. Following RFC 10008 Section 2.7, the cache key incorporates a SHA-256 digest of the request content and its representation metadata, so different query bodies are cached separately:

app.query(
  '/search',
  cache({
    cacheName: 'search-cache',
    cacheControl: 'max-age=3600',
  })
)

**Note**: To support this, the internal cache key format has changed for all methods, including GET. Cached entries are now stored under an internal URL of the form `/.hono/cache?__hono_cache_key=...`. If you purge cache entries by URL outside of the middleware (e.g. calling `caches.delete()` with the original request URL), you will need to update that logic. Existing cache entries stored with the old format will simply be re-fetched.

### ETag Middleware

The ETag Middleware now handles conditional requests for QUERY, returning `304 Not Modified` when `If-None-Match` matches.

### CORS Middleware

The CORS Middleware now includes QUERY in the default `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, which is now `GET, HEAD, PUT, POST, DELETE, PATCH, QUERY`. If you specify `allowMethods` explicitly, nothing changes for you.

Thanks [@usualoma](https://github.com/usualoma) and [@Cherry](https://github.com/Cherry)!

## Method Not Allowed Middleware

The new Method Not Allowed Middleware returns a `405 Method Not Allowed` response with a proper `Allow` header when the request path matches a registered route but the method does not:

import { methodNotAllowed } from 'hono/method-not-allowed'

const app \= new Hono()

app.use(methodNotAllowed({ app }))

app.get('/hello', (c) \=> c.text('Hello!'))
app.post('/hello', (c) \=> c.text('Posted!'))

// PUT /hello -> 405 Method Not Allowed
// Allow: GET, HEAD, POST

You can customize the response with the `onMethodNotAllowed` option:

app.use(
  methodNotAllowed({
    app,
    onMethodNotAllowed: (c, methods) \=>
      c.json({ error: 'Method Not Allowed' }, 405, { Allow: methods.join(', ') }),
  })
)

Thanks [@usualoma](https://github.com/usualoma)!

## RegExpRouter throws `UnsupportedPathError` at registration time

The RegExpRouter now detects unsupported path combinations when routes are registered, instead of at the first matching request. This means misconfigured routes fail fast at startup rather than at runtime. As a bonus, registration plus the first match is roughly 20% faster.

Thanks [@usualoma](https://github.com/usualoma)!

## Other improvements

*   `hono/utils/headers` has been synced with the IANA HTTP Field Name Registry, adding newly registered fields such as `Accept-Query`. Thanks [@akahoshi1421](https://github.com/akahoshi1421)!
*   The JWT and JWK middleware now accept a `realm` option for the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge on `401` responses, and challenge values are properly escaped. Thanks [@arhxam](https://github.com/arhxam)!
*   JSX: `useRef` and `RefObject` are now aligned with React 19. Note that this is a type-level change — `RefObject<T>` is now `{ current: T }`, so type a nullable ref as `RefObject<T | null>`, and pass `useRef(undefined)` instead of `useRef()`. Thanks [@ashunar0](https://github.com/ashunar0)!

# Releases · honojs/hono

Hono v4.13.0 is now available!

The highlight of this release is performance: a batch of low-level optimizations makes the core request/response path significantly faster — up to 1.25x on common routes in our benchmark. This release also adds first-class support for the HTTP QUERY method, defined in [RFC 10008](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10008.html), a new Method Not Allowed middleware, and more.

## Performance improvements

This release includes a series of small optimizations: skipping unnecessary `Headers` allocations, replacing regex tests with `indexOf`, allocating internal state lazily, and more.

Here is [`benchmarks/fetch`](https://github.com/honojs/hono/tree/main/benchmarks/fetch) comparing v4.12 and v4.13 (`ROUNDS=5 ./compare.sh`, Bun 1.4.0, Apple Silicon — each measurement runs in a fresh process, and the variant order is reversed every round to avoid warm-up bias):

Benchmark

v4.12

v4.13

Speedup

`ping` — `GET /`

165.83 ns

163.99 ns

1.01x

`query` — `GET /id/1?name=bun`

674.40 ns

616.99 ns

**1.09x**

`json` — `GET /user`

528.99 ns

422.44 ns

**1.25x**

`body` — `POST /json`

1.16 µs

1.00 µs

**1.15x**

The individual changes:

*   perf(context): iterate the header record with `for..in` [#5118](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5118)
*   perf(url): replace regex tests with `indexOf` [#5121](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5121)
*   perf(context): skip `Headers` creation when there are no headers to merge [#5122](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5122)
*   perf(urls): refactor `tryDecodeURIComponent` [#5158](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5158)
*   perf(request): allocate `#validatedData` lazily [#5175](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5175)
*   perf(request): probe the body cache without allocating [#5176](https://github.com/honojs/hono/pull/5176)

In addition, the RegExpRouter rewrite described below makes route registration plus the first match roughly 20% faster.

Thanks [@kibertoad](https://github.com/kibertoad) for the contributions!

## First-class QUERY method support

The QUERY method — a safe, idempotent method that carries a request body — is now a first-class citizen in Hono. You can define QUERY handlers with `app.query()`:

const app \= new Hono()

app.query('/search', async (c) \=> {
  const conditions \= await c.req.json()
  return c.json(await search(conditions))
})

Thanks [@shellhaki](https://github.com/shellhaki)!

## QUERY support across built-in middleware

The built-in middleware has been updated to handle QUERY requests properly:

### Cache Middleware

The Cache Middleware now caches QUERY responses. Following RFC 10008 Section 2.7, the cache key incorporates a SHA-256 digest of the request content and its representation metadata, so different query bodies are cached separately:

app.query(
  '/search',
  cache({
    cacheName: 'search-cache',
    cacheControl: 'max-age=3600',
  })
)

**Note**: To support this, the internal cache key format has changed for all methods, including GET. Cached entries are now stored under an internal URL of the form `/.hono/cache?__hono_cache_key=...`. If you purge cache entries by URL outside of the middleware (e.g. calling `caches.delete()` with the original request URL), you will need to update that logic. Existing cache entries stored with the old format will simply be re-fetched.

### ETag Middleware

The ETag Middleware now handles conditional requests for QUERY, returning `304 Not Modified` when `If-None-Match` matches.

### CORS Middleware

The CORS Middleware now includes QUERY in the default `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, which is now `GET, HEAD, PUT, POST, DELETE, PATCH, QUERY`. If you specify `allowMethods` explicitly, nothing changes for you.

Thanks [@usualoma](https://github.com/usualoma) and [@Cherry](https://github.com/Cherry)!

## Method Not Allowed Middleware

The new Method Not Allowed Middleware returns a `405 Method Not Allowed` response with a proper `Allow` header when the request path matches a registered route but the method does not:

import { methodNotAllowed } from 'hono/method-not-allowed'

const app \= new Hono()

app.use(methodNotAllowed({ app }))

app.get('/hello', (c) \=> c.text('Hello!'))
app.post('/hello', (c) \=> c.text('Posted!'))

// PUT /hello -> 405 Method Not Allowed
// Allow: GET, HEAD, POST

You can customize the response with the `onMethodNotAllowed` option:

app.use(
  methodNotAllowed({
    app,
    onMethodNotAllowed: (c, methods) \=>
      c.json({ error: 'Method Not Allowed' }, 405, { Allow: methods.join(', ') }),
  })
)

Thanks [@usualoma](https://github.com/usualoma)!

## RegExpRouter throws `UnsupportedPathError` at registration time

The RegExpRouter now detects unsupported path combinations when routes are registered, instead of at the first matching request. This means misconfigured routes fail fast at startup rather than at runtime. As a bonus, registration plus the first match is roughly 20% faster.

Thanks [@usualoma](https://github.com/usualoma)!

## Other improvements

*   `hono/utils/headers` has been synced with the IANA HTTP Field Name Registry, adding newly registered fields such as `Accept-Query`. Thanks [@akahoshi1421](https://github.com/akahoshi1421)!
*   The JWT and JWK middleware now accept a `realm` option for the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge on `401` responses, and challenge values are properly escaped. Thanks [@arhxam](https://github.com/arhxam)!
*   JSX: `useRef` and `RefObject` are now aligned with React 19. Note that this is a type-level change — `RefObject<T>` is now `{ current: T }`, so type a nullable ref as `RefObject<T | null>`, and pass `useRef(undefined)` instead of `useRef()`. Thanks [@ashunar0](https://github.com/ashunar0)!
*   JSX: a function component can now return an array of children without throwing during server-side rendering. Thanks [@natsuki-engr](https://github.com/natsuki-engr)!
*   The Compress Middleware now sets `Vary: Accept-Encoding` on negotiated responses. Thanks [@arhxam](https://github.com/arhxam)!

# Build an app with Next.js and Bun - Bun

[Next.js](https://nextjs.org/) is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. It supports server-side rendering, static site generation, and API routes. Bun installs packages fast and can run Next.js development and production servers.

* * *

1

Create a new Next.js app

Use the interactive CLI to scaffold a new Next.js project and install its dependencies.

terminal

```
bun create next-app@latest my-bun-app
```

2

Start the dev server

Change to the project directory and run the dev server with Bun.

terminal

```
cd my-bun-app
bun --bun run dev
```

This starts the Next.js dev server with Bun’s runtime.Open [`http://localhost:3000`](http://localhost:3000) in your browser to see the result. Changes you make to `app/page.tsx` are hot-reloaded in the browser.

3

Update scripts in package.json

Prefix the Next.js CLI commands in your `package.json` scripts with `bun --bun` so that Bun executes the Next.js CLI for `dev`, `build`, and `start`.

package.json

```
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "bun --bun next dev", 
    "build": "bun --bun next build", 
    "start": "bun --bun next start", 
  }
}

# Reducing local dev time by 83%: Why we migrated off Next.js

At Inngest, DX is everything. Uniquely good, ergonomic APIs are why customers choose us, and stay with us. So it might not be surprising that every engineering decision follows the same checklist: **make it simple, make it obvious, make it delightful.** As such, it's nearly impossible to separate how we want devs to feel when using Inngest, from how we want our own team to feel when _building_ Inngest.

This is the story of how (and why) we migrated off Next.js.

## Early signals, and an attempt to make it work

When I arrived at Inngest nearly two years ago, the team had already gone all in on Next.js. They'd adopted the App Router while it was still in beta, [migrated from Vite in under a day](/blog/migrating-from-vite-to-nextjs?ref=blog-migrating-off-nextjs-tanstack-start), and embraced RSC as the future of React. At the time, the promise was compelling: escape the blank loading states and network waterfalls of SPAs, get nested layouts and streaming out of the box, and consolidate on a single framework.

But the honeymoon didn't last. Next.js optimizes for a specific workflow—dedicated frontend teams who live in the framework full-time. For us, a small team where most engineers wear many hats, the cognitive overhead was punishing. The "use client" / "use server" directives, the layered cache APIs, the muddy boundaries between RSC and client components—all of it added friction that compounded over time.

Engineers who didn't spend most of their week in the frontend found themselves constantly fighting the framework rather than shipping features.

### Backing away from RSC

As a first step, we tried just backing away from RSC in favor of a minimal use of vanilla server components and an overriding preference for client components. This helped, and made the developer experience mostly manageable, at least for a little while.

But then things got slow. _Really slow._ **Initial page load times for local development pushed 10-12 seconds minimum.** The drumbeat in Slack: "I HATE this." "The frontend is so SLOW".

Everyone now agreed: Our own developer experience _sucked_.

### Adding Turbopack and upgrading Next.js

In an effort to salvage things, we upgraded Next.js, and used Vercel's profiling tools to see if that might help. It didn't.

So we tried Turbopack. We tried it twice, in fact. No small feat for a codebase of our size. Each migration required dependency upgrades and refactoring. It also meant that our local development and production environments were different, because Vercel only supported Webpack for production builds at the time.

This did cause us a few issues, and unfortunately did not help the local load times much, shaving off only a couple seconds on average.

It seemed Turbopack was not, in fact, _turbo._ It was time to look outside Next.js.

## Evaluating alternatives

![Figure 1: Comparing Next.js and Tanstack Start](/_next/image?url=%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fmigrating-off-nextjs-tanstack-start%2Ffigure-1-performance-comparison.png&w=3840&q=95)

We needed faster local load times, a sensible router API, and clear conventions around server/client components. We prototyped three options: Tanstack Start, Deno Fresh, and React Router v7 (essentially Remix).

I'd used both Deno Fresh and Remix at previous startups for large, complex applications. Both are great. Deno's performant, Typescript-first runtime and opinionated tooling is particularly appealing. React Router is battle tested. However, Fresh's long delay between version 1 and 2 gave us pause, and Remix's decision to merge into React Router, and then again break itself out into a separate preview platform made us think. As for Tanstack Start? It was still in release candidate (and still is as I write this!)

Nevertheless, I built prototypes with each, checking off required integrations and features. All passed with varying to varying degrees of effect. No obvious disqualifiers.

## Choosing and migrating to Tanstack

![Figure 2: Migration timeline from prototype to deployment](/_next/image?url=%2Fassets%2Fblog%2Fmigrating-off-nextjs-tanstack-start%2Ffigure-2-migration-timeline.png&w=3840&q=95)

Ultimately, we decided to go with Tanstack Start. Maybe that sounds like an unusual choice given the context I shared, but the team had already used Tanstack's other offerings and were exceedingly optimistic about its direction.

When developer experience matters, having excited developers matters.

### Incremental, or brute force?

The next choice was whether we wanted to do this incrementally, or rip off the bandaid all at once.

**The brute force** **option** would be a question of time and resources. Auth and integrations were sorted during prototyping, but the unknown was route conversion effort.

**An incremental** **approach** would require conditional routing and imports from our shared component library, which leaned heavily on Next.js utilities. More infrastructure work.

To decide, I'd have to get a handle on the conversion effort of our typical routes. And the only way to really estimate that would be to try some.

### Ripping the bandaid off

We had two Next.js app heads, one for our dev server and one for our dashboard.

**The Dev Server** has a small subset of the dashboard routes so I started there, converting a few. To my surprise, that process went fast enough that I simply pressed on and converted them all in a few days. All in, the bandaid came off for the dev server in about a week.

For all of our shared components, I simply made copies wherever we used Next.js and used Tanstack equivalents. There were a few hiccups where our app heads referenced each other through our shared component library, but a few not-terrible interim type hacks made quick work of those.

**The dashboard,** on the other hand, took longer. More routes, more complexity. This stretched the project a bit longer, but it was still only a couple weeks of engineering effort for one engineer (with the help of AI).

## The results

Post migration, our DX is _dramatically_ better. We rarely see initial local page load times go beyond 2-3 seconds, and that is always only on the first of **any** route loaded. All routes after the first are almost always instant in Tanstack. Unlike Next.js where the first local load of any given route is always slow. The drumbeat in Slack is now, "I cannot believe how snappy it is!"

### Technical tradeoffs

There's a full breakdown on technical tradeoffs in this handy [comparison matrix](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/comparison), but for us, the core difference came down to trading Next.js's convention-over-configuration approach. For us, a small team where most engineers wear many hats, the cognitive overhead was punishing. Engineers who didn't spend most of their week in the frontend found themselves constantly fighting the framework rather than shipping features.

Everyone now agreed: Our own developer experience _sucked_.

# Research: Migrating Next.js 16 App Router → TanStack Start + Hono + Bun (2025–2026)

**Baseline:** Next.js 16 released 2025-10-21/22 (stable Turbopack, Cache Components, React 19.2). Your app (Next 16.3 + React 19 + Tailwind 4, REST + SSE to FastAPI) is a client-heavy dashboard — exactly the profile that migration evidence says gains least from App Router's server-first model.

## Summary
TanStack Start went stable v1.0 on 2026-03-18 after a Sep 2025 RC, is built on Vite + Nitro (not Hono), and now has first-party migration docs plus two notable production migrations (Inngest, Railway). Hono (v4.13.0, Aug 2026) is mature and standalone — typically used *alongside* TanStack Start (its Nitro server) for the API layer, not inside it. Bun (1.3.14 stable; 1.4.0 Rust rewrite in canary) runs both Hono and Next.js dev, but has known SSE idle-timeout and native-addon gaps. A staged migration (frontend-first, keep FastAPI) is defensible; a full swap is not yet low-risk.

## Findings

### 1. TanStack Start — production readiness
1. **Version/status:** RC announced 2025-09-22; v1.0 tagged 2026-03-18. Current packages ~1.168.35 (Aug 3, 2026); `@tanstack/start` ~11k weekly downloads. Fast release cadence (weekly bumps) is itself a risk. [RC blog](https://tanstack.com/blog/announcing-tanstack-start-v1), [release stream](https://github.com/TanStack/router/releases/tag/release-2026-08-03-2216) *(high confidence)*
2. **Runtime:** Runs on **Vite + Nitro** — TanStack explicitly ditched Vinxi adapters ("TanStack Start = Nitro + Vite + TanStack Router"). Not Hono. SSR streaming, middleware, typed loaders, `createServerFn`, and file-based server routes are all first-class. [Why TanStack Start is Ditching Adapters](https://tanstack.com/blog/why-tanstack-start-is-ditching-adapters), [Nitro SSR example](https://nitro.build/examples/vite-ssr-tss-react) *(high)*
3. **Model vs Next:** Isomorphic-by-default — all code runs both sides unless wrapped in `createServerFn` (opposite of Next's server-by-default RSC). Data loading = route loaders + TanStack Query (fits your charts/SSE dashboard well). RSC exists only as experimental `@tanstack/react-start-rsc` (0.1.x). [Official comparison](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/comparison), [migration skill](https://github.com/tanstack/router/blob/main/packages/react-start/skills/lifecycle/migrate-from-nextjs/SKILL.md) *(high)*
4. **Production evidence:** Inngest migrated off Next.js to TanStack Start (blog 2026-01-30): local page loads 10–12s → 2–3s, 83% local dev time reduction, ~3 weeks one engineer — while Start was still RC. [Inngest blog](https://www.inngest.com/blog/migrating-off-nextjs-tanstack-start) *(high)*. Railway moved 200+ routes off Next.js in two PRs (builds 10+ min → <2 min) but to **Vite + TanStack Router**, not Start. [Railway blog](https://blog.railway.com/p/moving-railways-frontend-off-nextjs) *(medium — not the same stack)*
5. **Gaps:** no built-in image optimization (migration guide prescribes `@unpic/react`); auth is DIY (official session/OAuth/CSRF guide exists); ecosystem/plugins much smaller than Next. [Migrate from Next.js guide](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/migrate-from-next-js), [auth server primitives](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/guide/authentication-server-primitives) *(high)*

### 2. Hono — server layer
6. **Version:** v4.13.0 (2026-08-03) — core perf up to 1.25x, QUERY method, Method-Not-Allowed middleware. v4.12.4 (2026-03-03) fixed an **SSE injection vulnerability** (CR/LF in `event`/`id`/`retry`; GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr) — pin ≥4.12.4. [Releases](https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.0), [v4.12.4](https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.12.4) *(high)*
7. **Capabilities:** JSX with async components + Suspense, SSG, Client Components, `streamSSE` helper, WebSocket helper with adapters for Bun, Node (`@hono/node-server`), Deno, Cloudflare Workers/Pages. Middleware ecosystem is solid (auth, JWT, cache, ETag, CORS, rate-limit). [JSX](https://hono.dev/docs/guides/jsx), [WebSocket helper](https://hono.dev/docs/helpers/websocket) *(high)*
8. **Standalone vs inside Start:** TanStack Start's server is Nitro; Hono is not part of it. Community pattern = TanStack Start for SSR + Hono as the API layer (via Nitro handler or standalone); community repo shows wiring Hono into Start's request handler. [isnifer/tanstack-start-ssr-hono](https://github.com/isnifer/tanstack-start-ssr-hono) *(medium — community, not official)*

### 3. Bun — runtime
9. **Version:** 1.2 on 2025-01-22; stable **1.3.14** (2026-05-13, HTTP/3 in Bun.serve, Bun.cron). **1.4.0 is a full Zig→Rust rewrite, in canary (announced 2026-07-08); Bun was acquired by Anthropic Dec 2025** — runtime churn to monitor before committing. [Bun 1.2](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.2), [Rust rewrite](https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust) *(high)*
10. **Next.js compat:** `bun --bun next dev/build/start` is officially documented; Vercel added a native Bun runtime (beta) via `bunVersion` in vercel.json. So Bun *can* run your current Next 16 app, but it's secondary support, not the blessed path. [Bun + Next.js guide](https://bun.sh/docs/guides/ecosystem/nextjs), [Vercel Bun beta](https://bun.sh/blog/vercel-adds-native-bun-support) *(high)*
11. **Performance:** Hono's own benchmarks show ~64k req/s (Bun) vs ~27k (Node) on bun-http-framework-benchmark, but third-party runs show variance — one macOS/Windows test found Node+Hono faster. `@hono/node-server` README shows ~85k req/s (Node). Treat "Bun is always faster" as workload-dependent. [Hono benchmarks](https://hono.dev/docs/concepts/benchmarks), [oven discussion #21998](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/21998), [node-server](https://github.com/honojs/node-server/) *(medium)*
12. **Known production issues:** native addons (e.g., bcrypt) are the main blocker (JavaScriptCore vs V8); npm packages with node-assuming postinstall scripts; `node:` compat is high but not 100%. [Node compat docs](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat), [production write-up](https://abrarqasim.com/blog/bun-1-in-production-six-months-of-tradeoffs/) *(medium — anecdotal)*

### 4. Migration evidence & pain points
13. **Guides:** official [Migrate from Next.js](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/migrate-from-next-js) covers route conversion, API mapping, Server Actions → `createServerFn`, middleware, data fetching; third-party [Dev Encyclopedia guide](https://devencyclopedia.com/blog/nextjs-to-tanstack-start-migration) aggregates Railway/Inngest lessons. *(high)*
14. **Pain points reported:** isomorphic-by-default confusion; bundling leaks between client/server; image optimization (`next/image` → Unpic); auth reimplementation; and dev-mode vs prod-behavior differences (Inngest warns "don't rely on dev mode alone"). No i18n story found in Start docs — gap. [Inngest blog](https://www.inngest.com/blog/migrating-off-nextjs-tanstack-start), [SKILL.md](https://github.com/tanstack/router/blob/main/packages/react-start/skills/lifecycle/migrate-from-nextjs/SKILL.md) *(high)*

### 5. SSE on Hono/TanStack Start + Bun
15. **Hono SSE is production-usable** (`streamSSE` + abort handling) with Bun's native WebSocket/stream support, but three real gotchas: (a) `Bun.serve` **default idleTimeout ~10s kills quiet SSE streams** — must set `idleTimeout: 0` and/or keepalives [bun issue #27479](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/27479); (b) Hono `streamSSE` closes without periodic writes unless you `sleep` between events [hono issue #2050](https://github.com/honojs/hono/issues/2050); (c) Bun 1.1.26/1.1.27 had SSE disconnect/regression bugs (fixed later) [issue #13811](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/13811). Bun handles long-lived connections OK **with explicit timeouts/keepalives**; proxies (Fly.io) add their own idle limits — send heartbeats. [Bun SSE guide](https://bun.com/docs/guides/http/sse), [Fly.io post](https://ryanlabouve.com/writing/sse-streaming-on-fly/) *(high)*

## Recommended migration posture: **Staged, frontend-first — not a full swap**
- **Keep the FastAPI backend (REST + SSE) as-is** — it's already runtime-agnostic and none of the frameworks improve it; SSE heartbeats + `idleTimeout` config are required regardless of framework.
- **Stage 1 (low risk, now):** run existing Next 16.3 dev/build on Bun (`bun --bun next dev`) to capture Bun DX/perf with zero migration; pin Hono ≥4.12.4 only if you extract the SSE proxy/BFF layer.
- **Stage 2 (pilot):** prototype 1–2 dashboard routes in TanStack Start (loaders + `createServerFn` + TanStack Query) alongside the Next app; Inngest/Railway show this is the winning pattern for client-heavy, real-time UIs, and official migration docs now exist.
- **Stage 3 (commit):** only after the pilot and after Bun 1.4 (Rust) stabilizes — or keep Node as the Start/Hono runtime if native-addon or SSE issues bite. The main blocker is not maturity of any single piece but the combination's novelty: TanStack Start v1 is ~5 months old, Bun 1.4 is a runtime rewrite in progress, and Hono-in-Start is community-shaped, not official.

## Gaps
- No benchmark found for TanStack Start SSR on Bun vs Node (request/sec, cold start) — only framework-level Hono benchmarks.
- No production reports of TanStack Start + Hono + Bun as a *combined* stack; evidence covers pairs.
- TanStack Start i18n and caching semantics (ISR-equivalent) vs Next 16 Cache Components are undocumented; needs hands-on validation.
- Railway migrated to TanStack Router (SPA) — does not validate Start SSR in production at scale.

## Sources
- Kept: [TanStack Start v1 RC](https://tanstack.com/blog/announcing-tanstack-start-v1); [Ditching Adapters](https://tanstack.com/blog/why-tanstack-start-is-ditching-adapters); [Start vs Next](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/comparison); [Migrate from Next.js](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/migrate-from-next-js); [Inngest migration](https://www.inngest.com/blog/migrating-off-nextjs-tanstack-start); [Railway migration](https://blog.railway.com/p/moving-railways-frontend-off-nextjs); [Hono releases](https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases); [Hono SSE vuln v4.12.4](https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.12.4); [Hono benchmarks](https://hono.dev/docs/concepts/benchmarks); [Bun 1.2](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.2); [Bun Rust rewrite](https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust); [Bun+Next.js](https://bun.sh/docs/guides/ecosystem/nextjs); [Bun SSE guide](https://bun.com/docs/guides/http/sse); [bun#27479](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/27479); [hono#2050](https://github.com/honojs/hono/issues/2050); [Next.js 16](https://nextjs.org/blog/next-16).
- Dropped: InfoQ/MakerKit/Medium roundups (aggregated, no primary numbers); LinkedIn benchmark post (unverifiable methodology); npm pages (403/version churn not useful vs GitHub releases).

**Baseline:** Next.js 16 released 2025-10-21/22 (stable Turbopack, Cache Components, React 19.2). Your app (Next 16.3 + React 19 + Tailwind 4, REST + SSE to FastAPI) is a client-heavy dashboard — exactly the profile that migration evidence says gains least from App Router's server-first model.

## Summary
TanStack Start went stable v1.0 on 2026-03-18 after a Sep 2025 RC, is built on Vite + Nitro (not Hono), and now has first-party migration docs plus two notable production migrations (Inngest, Railway). Hono (v4.13.0, Aug 2026) is mature and standalone — typically used *alongside* TanStack Start (its Nitro server) for the API layer, not inside it. Bun (1.3.14 stable; 1.4.0 Rust rewrite in canary) runs both Hono and Next.js dev, but has known SSE idle-timeout and native-addon gaps. A staged migration (frontend-first, keep FastAPI) is defensible; a full swap is not yet low-risk.

## Findings

### 1. TanStack Start — production readiness
1. **Version/status:** RC announced 2025-09-22; v1.0 tagged 2026-03-18. Current packages ~1.168.35 (Aug 3, 2026); `@tanstack/start` ~11k weekly downloads. Fast release cadence (weekly bumps) is itself a risk. [RC blog](https://tanstack.com/blog/announcing-tanstack-start-v1), [release stream](https://github.com/TanStack/router/releases/tag/release-2026-08-03-2216) *(high confidence)*
2. **Runtime:** Runs on **Vite + Nitro** — TanStack explicitly ditched Vinxi adapters ("TanStack Start = Nitro + Vite + TanStack Router"). Not Hono. SSR streaming, middleware, typed loaders, `createServerFn`, and file-based server routes are all first-class. [Why TanStack Start is Ditching Adapters](https://tanstack.com/blog/why-tanstack-start-is-ditching-adapters), [Nitro SSR example](https://nitro.build/examples/vite-ssr-tss-react) *(high)*
3. **Model vs Next:** Isomorphic-by-default — all code runs both sides unless wrapped in `createServerFn` (opposite of Next's server-by-default RSC). Data loading = route loaders + TanStack Query (fits your charts/SSE dashboard well). RSC exists only as experimental `@tanstack/react-start-rsc` (0.1.x). [Official comparison](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/comparison), [migration skill](https://github.com/tanstack/router/blob/main/packages/react-start/skills/lifecycle/migrate-from-nextjs/SKILL.md) *(high)*
4. **Production evidence:** Inngest migrated off Next.js to TanStack Start (blog 2026-01-30): local page loads 10–12s → 2–3s, 83% local dev time reduction, ~3 weeks one engineer — while Start was still RC. [Inngest blog](https://www.inngest.com/blog/migrating-off-nextjs-tanstack-start) *(high)*. Railway moved 200+ routes off Next.js in two PRs (builds 10+ min → <2 min) but to **Vite + TanStack Router**, not Start. [Railway blog](https://blog.railway.com/p/moving-railways-frontend-off-nextjs) *(medium — not the same stack)*
5. **Gaps:** no built-in image optimization (migration guide prescribes `@unpic/react`); auth is DIY (official session/OAuth/CSRF guide exists); ecosystem/plugins much smaller than Next. [Migrate from Next.js guide](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/migrate-from-next-js), [auth server primitives](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/guide/authentication-server-primitives) *(high)*

### 2. Hono — server layer
6. **Version:** v4.13.0 (2026-08-03) — core perf up to 1.25x, QUERY method, Method-Not-Allowed middleware. v4.12.4 (2026-03-03) fixed an **SSE injection vulnerability** (CR/LF in `event`/`id`/`retry`; GHSA-p6xx-57qc-3wxr) — pin ≥4.12.4. [Releases](https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.0), [v4.12.4](https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.12.4) *(high)*
7. **Capabilities:** JSX with async components + Suspense, SSG, Client Components, `streamSSE` helper, WebSocket helper with adapters for Bun, Node (`@hono/node-server`), Deno, Cloudflare Workers/Pages. Middleware ecosystem is solid (auth, JWT, cache, ETag, CORS, rate-limit). [JSX](https://hono.dev/docs/guides/jsx), [WebSocket helper](https://hono.dev/docs/helpers/websocket) *(high)*
8. **Standalone vs inside Start:** TanStack Start's server is Nitro; Hono is not part of it. Community pattern = TanStack Start for SSR + Hono as the API layer (via Nitro handler or standalone); community repo shows wiring Hono into Start's request handler. [isnifer/tanstack-start-ssr-hono](https://github.com/isnifer/tanstack-start-ssr-hono) *(medium — community, not official)*

### 3. Bun — runtime
9. **Version:** 1.2 on 2025-01-22; stable **1.3.14** (2026-05-13, HTTP/3 in Bun.serve, Bun.cron). **1.4.0 is a full Zig→Rust rewrite, in canary (announced 2026-07-08); Bun was acquired by Anthropic Dec 2025** — runtime churn to monitor before committing. [Bun 1.2](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.2), [Rust rewrite](https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust) *(high)*
10. **Next.js compat:** `bun --bun next dev/build/start` is officially documented; Vercel added a native Bun runtime (beta) via `bunVersion` in vercel.json. So Bun *can* run your current Next 16 app, but it's secondary support, not the blessed path. [Bun + Next.js guide](https://bun.sh/docs/guides/ecosystem/nextjs), [Vercel Bun beta](https://bun.sh/blog/vercel-adds-native-bun-support) *(high)*
11. **Performance:** Hono's own benchmarks show ~64k req/s (Bun) vs ~27k (Node) on bun-http-framework-benchmark, but third-party runs show variance — one macOS/Windows test found Node+Hono faster. `@hono/node-server` README shows ~85k req/s (Node). Treat "Bun is always faster" as workload-dependent. [Hono benchmarks](https://hono.dev/docs/concepts/benchmarks), [oven discussion #21998](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/discussions/21998), [node-server](https://github.com/honojs/node-server/) *(medium)*
12. **Known production issues:** native addons (e.g., bcrypt) are the main blocker (JavaScriptCore vs V8); npm packages with node-assuming postinstall scripts; `node:` compat is high but not 100%. [Node compat docs](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/nodejs-compat), [production write-up](https://abrarqasim.com/blog/bun-1-in-production-six-months-of-tradeoffs/) *(medium — anecdotal)*

### 4. Migration evidence & pain points
13. **Guides:** official [Migrate from Next.js](https://tanstack.com/start/latest/docs/framework/react/migrate-from-next-js) covers route conversion, API mapping, Server Actions → `createServerFn`, middleware, data fetching; third-party [Dev Encyclopedia guide](https://devencyclopedia.com/blog/nextjs-to-tanstack-start-migration) aggregates Railway/Inngest lessons. *(high)*
14. **Pain points reported:** isomorphic-by-default confusion; bundling leaks between client/server; image optimization (`next/image` → Unpic); auth reimplementation; and dev-mode vs prod-behavior differences (Inngest warns "don't rely on dev mode alone"). No i18n story found in Start docs — gap. [Inngest blog](https://www.inngest.com/blog/migrating-off-nextjs-tanstack-start), [SKILL.md](https://github.com/tanstack/router/blob/main/packages/react-start/skills/lifecycle/migrate-from-nextjs/SKILL.md) *(high)*

### 5. SSE on Hono/TanStack Start + Bun
15. **Hono SSE is production-usable** (`streamSSE` + abort handling) with Bun's native WebSocket/stream support, but three real gotchas: (a) `Bun.serve` **default idleTimeout ~10s kills quiet SSE streams** — must set `idleTimeout: 0` and/or keepalives [bun issue #27479](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/27479); (b) Hono `streamSSE` closes without periodic writes unless you `sleep` between events [hono issue #2050](https://github.com/honojs/hono/issues/2050); (c) Bun 1.1.26/1.1.27 had SSE disconnect/regression bugs (fixed later) [issue #13811](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/13811). Bun handles long-lived connections OK **with explicit timeouts/keepalives**; proxies (Fly.io) add their own idle limits — send heartbeats. [Bun SSE guide](https://bun.com/docs/guides/http/sse), [Fly.io post](https://ryanlabouve.com/writing/sse-streaming-on-fly/) *(high)*

## Recommended migration posture: **Staged, frontend-first — not a full swap**
- **Keep the FastAPI backend (REST + SSE) as-is** — it's already runtime-agnostic and none of the frameworks improve it; SSE heartbeats + `idleTimeout` config are required regardless of framework.
- **Stage 1 (low risk, now):** run existing Next 16.3 dev/build on Bun (`bun --bun next dev`) to capture Bun DX/perf with zero migration; pin Hono ≥4.12.4 only if you extract the SSE proxy/BFF layer.
- **Stage 2 (pilot):** prototype 1–2 dashboard routes in TanStack Start (loaders + `createServerFn` + TanStack Query) alongside the Next app; Inngest/Railway show this is the winning pattern for client-heavy, real-time UIs, and official migration docs now exist.
- **Stage 3 (commit):** only after the pilot and after Bun 1.4 (Rust) stabilizes — or keep Node as the Start/Hono runtime if native-addon or SSE issues bite. The main blocker is not maturity of any single piece but the combination's novelty: TanStack Start v1 is ~5 months old, Bun 1.4 is a runtime rewrite in progress, and Hono-in-Start is community-shaped, not official.

## Gaps
- No benchmark found for TanStack Start SSR on Bun vs Node (request/sec, cold start) — only framework-level Hono benchmarks.
- No production reports of TanStack Start + Hono + Bun as a *combined* stack; evidence covers pairs.
- TanStack Start i18n and caching semantics (ISR-equivalent) vs Next 16 Cache Components are undocumented; needs hands-on validation.
- Railway migrated to TanStack Router (SPA) — does not validate Start SSR in production at scale.

## Sources
